\chapter{The Verb That Takes Another Verb}
\label{ch:ru-want-can-must}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I want, put a bare infinitive after it with nothing in between, give the purpose of an action with chtoby, say what I can and cannot do, and state an obligation in a sentence with no subject at all.}

Fourteen infinitives had been taught and not one of them had ever stood after another verb, because the track had no khochu, mogu or nado to put one after: the pattern was missing, not the words. moch had been worse off than missing -- the pomogat lesson spelled out that the verb is po- plus moch and then never taught moch, so the reader had been reading it for fifteen chapters. nado closes the chapter on a sentence with no subject in it, which is the same freedom as the absent copula the track already teaches.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[khatét]{\ru{хотеть} — \textquotedblleft{}to want,\textquotedblright{} the verb the book has been missing}

\label{lesson:RU-C20-khotet}



\begin{quote}
Reach back four chapters, and then further.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{и}}, the one-letter joiner, and its old pointing stem
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{знать}}, English \emph{know}, and the \textbf{-\ru{у} / -\ru{ю}} that marks the \emph{I} form of almost every Russian verb
  \item \emph{Recall:} the comma at the seam of every clause hung under another
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{почему}}, which is \textbf{\ru{по}} plus a form of \textbf{\ru{что}}, and \emph{\ru{я} \ru{думаю}, \ru{что} …}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{хотеть}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{хотеть}} — \emph{khatét} — \textbf{to want}
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{хочу}} — \emph{ya khachú} — \textbf{I want}
  \item \textbf{\ru{ты} \ru{хочешь}} — \emph{ty khóchesh} — \textbf{you want}
\end{itemize}

Look at the \emph{I} form. The \textbf{\ru{т}} of the infinitive has turned into a \textbf{\ru{ч}} — the same consonant swap you met in the first verbs — and the ending is the familiar \textbf{-\ru{у}}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{хочу} \ru{чай}} — \emph{ya khachú chai} — I want tea.
\end{itemize}

This book has taught you to say what you do, what you know, what you understand and what you love. Until this line it could not say what you \textbf{want}, which is the first thing a traveller needs and the last thing this book supplied.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{хотеть}} is native Slavic and stops there. There is no secure Latin cousin, no Germanic one, no English one — the etymologists trace it inside the Slavic family and no further.

That is the third time this book has had to say so, after \textbf{\ru{но}} and \textbf{\ru{сок}}, and the pattern behind it is worth noticing: the words a language never borrows are the ones it needs every day.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{хотеть}}, then \emph{\ru{я} \ru{хочу}}, and hear the \textbf{\ru{т}} turn into \textbf{\ru{ч}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{хочу} \ru{чай}}
  \item \emph{Build:} name a drink or a food you own and say you want it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I want tea.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{хочу} \ru{чай}}.) Which letter changes between \textbf{\ru{хотеть}} and \textbf{\ru{хочу}}? (The \textbf{\ru{т}} becomes \textbf{\ru{ч}}.) Does this verb have an English cousin? (\textbf{No} — it is native Slavic and traceable no further.) And one look back: which verb means \emph{to know}, and what is its English cousin? (That is \textbf{\ru{знать}}, and the cousin is \emph{know}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ya khachú chitát]{\ru{я} \ru{хочу} \ru{читать} — two verbs in a row, and no word between them}

\label{lesson:RU-C20-khochu-chitat}



\begin{quote}
Yesterday's verb, and one from a long way back.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{хотеть}}, with no cousin outside Slavic, and \emph{\ru{я} \ru{хочу}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{говорить}}, which is \textbf{not} related to \emph{govern}, and the two verb families Russian sorts its endings into
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{и}} joining two whole clauses
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{потому} \ru{что}}, and the comma that stands in front of the pair
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{быть}} and \emph{\ru{жить}}, the first two verbs, and the root behind \emph{\ru{жить}} that means \textbf{quick}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the infinitive finally has somewhere to stand}]
This book has taught you fourteen verbs, and every one of them arrived in its \textbf{infinitive} — \emph{\ru{читать}}, \emph{\ru{писать}}, \emph{\ru{говорить}}, the dictionary form ending in \textbf{-\ru{ть}}. Until now that form has had nothing to do except be the name of the verb.

Put it straight after a finite verb and it goes to work:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{хочу} \ru{читать}} — \emph{ya khachú chitát} — I want \textbf{to read}.
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{хочу} \ru{писать}} — \emph{ya khachú pisát} — I want \textbf{to write}.
\end{itemize}

Count the words between the two verbs: \textbf{none}. English needs \emph{to}; Russian needs nothing at all. The second verb simply stays in the form you learned it in.

That single fact turns every infinitive in this book into something you can say you want to do, which is fourteen new sentences from one pattern.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{хочу} \ru{читать}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{хочу} \ru{говорить}}
  \item \emph{Build:} run through the verbs you own, each one after \emph{\ru{я} \ru{хочу}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What goes between the two verbs in \emph{\ru{я} \ru{хочу} \ru{читать}}? (\textbf{Nothing} — Russian has no word for English's \emph{to}.) Which form does the second verb take? (\textbf{The infinitive}, exactly as the book taught it.) And one look back: is \emph{\ru{говорить}} related to English \emph{govern}? (\textbf{No} — the resemblance is an accident.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shtóby]{\ru{чтобы} — \textquotedblleft{}in order to,\textquotedblright{} which is \ru{что} wearing a wish}

\label{lesson:RU-C20-chtoby}



\begin{quote}
The very first word in the book, and one of the joiners.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{привет}}, the word you opened with
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{понимать}}, whose root means \textbf{to take hold of}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{или}}, built from \textbf{\ru{и}} plus \textbf{\ru{ли}}, and the comma at every seam
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{видеть}}, and \emph{\ru{когда}} on the same ancient question-stem as \emph{\ru{как}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{видеть}}'s cousin \emph{wit}, the consonant that swaps in \emph{\ru{я} \ru{вижу}}, and the \textbf{\ru{г}} that is sometimes said as a \textbf{\ru{в}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — a purpose is a wish with \ru{что} on the front}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{чтобы}} — \emph{shtóby} — \textbf{in order to, so that}
\end{itemize}

Two pieces, both nearly yours: \textbf{\ru{что}}, and \textbf{\ru{бы}}, the small particle Russian puts on anything that is wished for rather than done. A purpose, in Russian, is literally a \emph{that}-clause said in the mood of a wish.

Put an infinitive after it and you have your reason for doing something:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{читаю}, \ru{чтобы} \ru{понимать}} — \emph{ya chitáyu, shtóby panimát} — I read \textbf{in order to} understand.
\end{itemize}

The comma before \textbf{\ru{чтобы}} is compulsory, like every subordinator's. The verb after it is the infinitive, exactly as after \textbf{\ru{хочу}} — so the pattern you learned in the last lesson is doing a second job here without changing.

Note the stress: \textbf{\ru{чтобы}} is stressed on its \textbf{first} syllable, unlike \textbf{\ru{что}}, which has only one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{читаю}, \ru{чтобы} \ru{понимать}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{чтобы}} with the stress on the front — \emph{SHTÓ-by}
  \item \emph{Build:} something you do, a comma, \textbf{\ru{чтобы}}, and the reason you do it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two pieces make \textbf{\ru{чтобы}}? (\textbf{\ru{что}} plus \textbf{\ru{бы}}.) What form of the verb follows it? (\textbf{The infinitive}.) Which syllable carries the stress? (\textbf{The first}.) And one look back: what was the very first word in this book? (That was \textbf{\ru{привет}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[moch]{\ru{мочь} — \textquotedblleft{}can,\textquotedblright{} and you have been reading it for fifteen chapters}

\label{lesson:RU-C20-moch}



\begin{quote}
Two verbs from the early chapters, and one pattern.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{идти}}, the one-way verb whose past comes from a different root
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{помогать}}, and the fact that its second half was a verb meaning \textbf{to be able}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{ни} … \ru{ни} …}, standing in front of both halves
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{когда}} joining two clauses, with the comma at the seam
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{мочь}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{мочь}} — \emph{moch} — \textbf{to be able, can}
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{могу}} — \emph{ya magú} — \textbf{I can}
  \item \textbf{\ru{ты} \ru{можешь}} — \emph{ty mózhesh} — \textbf{you can}
\end{itemize}

You have seen this word already. When the book took \textbf{\ru{помогать}} apart it said in so many words that the verb is \textbf{\ru{по}-} plus \textbf{\ru{мочь}}, \textquotedblleft{}to be able\textquotedblright{} — and then moved on without ever giving \textbf{\ru{мочь}} a lesson of its own. It is here now.

Like \textbf{\ru{хотеть}}, it takes a bare infinitive after it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{могу} \ru{читать}} — \emph{ya magú chitát} — I can read.
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{могу} \ru{идти}} — \emph{ya ne magú idtí} — I cannot go.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{мочь}} is PIE \textbf{*mag\textsuperscript{h}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to be able, to have power\textquotedblright{} — and the English descendants are three of the plainest words in the language:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{may} — permission, which began as ability
  \item \textbf{might} — both the verb and the noun meaning \emph{strength}
  \item \textbf{main}, as in \emph{with might and main}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{\ru{я} \ru{могу}} and \emph{I may} are, underneath, the same sentence. Russian kept the whole verb; English wore it down into a modal that no longer conjugates at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{могу} \ru{читать}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{могу} \ru{идти}}
  \item \emph{Build:} something you can do, then the same thing denied
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I can read.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{могу} \ru{читать}}.) Which taught verb has this one inside it? (That is \textbf{\ru{помогать}} — \emph{\ru{по}-} plus \emph{\ru{мочь}}.) Name two English words from the same root. (\emph{May}, \emph{might} — or \emph{main}.) What form follows it? (\textbf{The infinitive}, with nothing in between.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[náda]{\ru{надо} — a whole sentence with nobody in it}

\label{lesson:RU-C20-nado}



\begin{quote}
The verb of the mind, and the two newest words.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{думать}}, the verb inside the name of the Russian parliament, and its partner verb
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{мочь}}, English \emph{may} and \emph{might}, and \emph{\ru{тоже}} with \textbf{\ru{не}} after it
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{надо}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{надо}} — \emph{náda} — \textbf{it is necessary, one must}
\end{itemize}

Stress the first syllable; the \textbf{\ru{о}} at the end is unstressed and says \emph{a}, so the word comes out \emph{NÁ-da}.

Like \textbf{\ru{хотеть}} and \textbf{\ru{мочь}}, it is followed by a bare infinitive:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{надо} \ru{читать}} — \emph{náda chitát} — one must read.
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the sentence with no subject}]
Look at \textbf{\ru{надо} \ru{читать}} again and count the people in it. There are none.

There is no \textbf{\ru{я}}, no \textbf{\ru{ты}}, and no verb agreeing with anybody. English cannot do this: it has to invent a subject — \emph{one} must read, \emph{it} is necessary, \emph{you} should read — because an English sentence is not allowed to go without one.

Russian is allowed. \textbf{\ru{надо}} is an \textbf{impersonal} word: the obligation is simply stated, hanging in the air, belonging to nobody in particular. This is the same freedom you met when the present tense of \textbf{\ru{быть}} turned out to be missing altogether — Russian is content to leave out what it does not need.

Naming the person who must do it needs a case this book has not opened yet, so for now the impersonal form is the whole of it — and it is genuinely useful on its own.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{надо} \ru{читать}} — \emph{NÁ-da}, first syllable
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{надо} \ru{думать}}
  \item \emph{Build:} three things one must do, using verbs you own
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many people are named in \emph{\ru{надо} \ru{читать}}? (\textbf{None} — it is impersonal.) What must English add that Russian does not? (\textbf{A subject} — \emph{one}, \emph{it}, or \emph{you}.) Which other missing word does that remind you of? (\textbf{The present tense of \ru{быть}}, which Russian also leaves out.) And one look back: which council is named after the verb \emph{to think}? (\textbf{The Duma}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
